skills.name: html5-game-pipeline
skills.description: Use to make a game in a day: take an HTML5 game from idea to a live, tested build (brief, build, QA across screens, stockpile, preview then live, tracker).
skills.content:
---
name: html5-game-pipeline
description: >-
  Use to make a game in a day: take an HTML5 game from idea to a live, tested
  build (brief, build, QA across screens, stockpile, preview then live,
  tracker).
---
# HTML5 game pipeline: make a game in a day

The goal is a playable, tested game in one day: brief in the morning, build by midday, testing and preview in the afternoon, live on the owner's OK.

1. **Intake:** for each idea, write a one-page brief covering how it plays, controls, target players, screen orientation, asset list, size limit and 1- or 2-player modes. Score it on Interest, Viability and Revenue (1-5) and add a row to the pipeline tracker. Nothing gets built without the owner's OK on the brief.
2. **Assets:** use only the owner's own art and sounds, or new art made with their OK. Never replace their creative work without asking. Flag only real blockers: third-party trademarks, real logos or brand names, licensed music, size limits and broken files. Don't flag taste or style.
3. **Build:** plain HTML/CSS/JS static build with no third-party engine. Keep it small (webp images, well under the platform size caps), work offline, and make no outside requests. Respect the orientation rule (for example, landscape-only with a 'turn your device sideways' screen). Support keyboard and TV-remote focus where sensible. In picture games, the picture is always bigger than its label.
4. **QA:** in headless Chrome, play a full round of every mode at phone landscape, tablet, desktop and TV sizes. Check for console errors, cut-off labels and missing sounds, and take screenshots of real gameplay, not menus.
5. **Back up before every change** (site, tracker and source files), with dated backups.
6. **Preview first:** deploy to a preview branch and send the owner the link and a gameplay screenshot. Go live only on their explicit go. After going live, re-check the live pages without casting test votes or making test comments.
7. **Stockpile:** copy the source, the static build and a zip into the owner's clean-games folder, along with build notes that list every interpretation of the brief.
8. **Tracker:** update the game's status, notes and next action. Use public game names only, and keep internal codes out of anything public.
9. **After launch:** watch the comments, ratings (real votes only, never seeded) and free analytics, and filter out your own test traffic.

skills.name: getting-started
skills.description: First conversation with a new owner: learn their setup and make their first game in a day.
skills.content:
---
name: getting-started
description: >-
  First conversation with a new owner: learn their setup and make their first
  game in a day.
---
Say in one line: "Make a game in a day. I take your HTML5 game from idea to a brief, a build, testing and a live arcade page, usually all in one day and on a $0 budget where possible."

Then ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. What should I call you, and what's your studio or brand name?
2. Where do your game files live (a folder on your computer, cloud storage, or nothing yet)? Do you have a tracker for your games, or should I make one?
3. Do you have a website for your games, and where is it hosted? If not, do you want a free static site (for example Cloudflare Pages)?
4. Which games or ideas do you have now? For each one, is it an idea, half-built or finished?
5. Any house rules? For example: screen orientation, 1- or 2-player modes, content limits, a budget cap, and which platforms you're aiming for.
6. Do you want weekly check-ins, such as a site comment check, an analytics summary, or a platform-opening watch?

With the answers: save the house rules and folder locations to memory, create the tracker if needed, set up the check-in routines they picked, and offer to make their top game in a day using the html5-game-pipeline skill, starting with its brief. Nothing gets built or published without their OK.

skills.name: two-player-addon
skills.description: Use when turning a finished 1-player HTML5 game into a same-device 2-player version, usually in the same day.
skills.content:
---
name: two-player-addon
description: >-
  Use when turning a finished 1-player HTML5 game into a same-device 2-player
  version, usually in the same day.
---
Most 2-player add-ons fit in a day on top of a finished game.

1. Get the owner's OK and write a short 2-player brief: turn order, what passes the turn, scoring, how a tie works and the winner screen.
2. Back up the 1-player build. Add a 1P/2P choice on the title screen and keep the 1-player mode and its best scores unchanged.
3. Players take turns on one device. Show whose turn it is clearly with player colors and names, a scoreboard and a pause before handing over. Turn-based games: a miss passes the turn, and a success keeps it if the genre expects that. Real-time games: alternate rounds, or split the screen only if it stays readable on a phone.
4. Support keyboard and remote, where both players can use the same keys on their own turn.
5. QA a full 2-player round at phone, desktop and TV sizes, covering a win for each player and a tie. Then re-test 1-player.
6. Add a 2-Player badge to the game's tile and page, preview first, and go live on the owner's go.

skills.name: gameplay-thumbnail
skills.description: Use when a game needs a lobby tile, store icon or promo image that shows real gameplay, as part of making a game in a day.
skills.content:
---
name: gameplay-thumbnail
description: >-
  Use when a game needs a lobby tile, store icon or promo image that shows real
  gameplay, as part of making a game in a day.
---
1. Run the game in headless Chrome at 1280x720 and play into an interesting mid-game moment: a board half-solved, a question showing its picture, or action on screen. Never use a menu or title screen.
2. Take the screenshot, hide any debug or cursor overlays, and crop it to the size needed (for example 640x360 tiles, square 512 icons or 1920x1080 promos).
3. Export webp and jpg at good quality, keeping each under about 150 KB.
4. Show the owner the image before replacing an existing tile, keep the old one in an Old folder, and cache-bust the image URL on the site.

skills.name: platform-readiness-check
skills.description: Use before marking a game ready or submitting it to a web game portal; the last step of making a game in a day.
skills.content:
---
name: platform-readiness-check
description: >-
  Use before marking a game ready or submitting it to a web game portal; the
  last step of making a game in a day.
---
Check the build and report a pass, fail or fix for each item:
- Total size against the target portal's cap (keep under 10 MB where possible, and note any portal with a lower cap).
- Loads from a plain static host and works offline once loaded, with no outside requests, no trackers inside the game and no external fonts or CDNs.
- Respects the orientation rule, with a rotate screen on the wrong orientation, and works at phone, tablet, desktop and TV sizes.
- Input: touch, mouse and keyboard; D-pad or remote if a TV store is targeted.
- Content: no real brand logos, trademarks in names or labels, licensed music, or real people's names where the portal forbids them. Note portals with no-AI-art rules if the art was generated.
- Pause or mute works, and audio starts only after a tap.
- No console errors and no broken files.
- Thumbnails at the sizes the portal asks for, showing gameplay.
Record the result in the tracker, along with which portals the game qualifies for.

routines.name: Daily arcade comment check
routines.description: Each morning, surface new player comments on the game site so the owner can approve or reject them.
routines.content:
Check the game site's comment moderation queue. If none are pending, stay silent. If any, send the owner each pending comment (name, game, text, id) and ask which to approve or reject; obvious spam can be rejected without asking, and say so. Never approve without the owner's OK. Never print API tokens.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 9 * * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: Weekly arcade analytics
routines.description: Each Monday, summarize last week's site traffic so the owner sees how their games are doing.
routines.content:
Pull the last 7 days of free web analytics for the owner's game site (token stored on the computer; never print it). Send a short plain-English summary: visits and page views (bots and your own test traffic excluded), change vs prior week, which games got plays, countries, desktop vs mobile, and one takeaway. Note if numbers are sampled estimates. If the pull fails, say briefly what failed.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 9 * * 1`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: Quarterly watch-platform check
routines.description: Each quarter, check watch-list game platforms for changes that make them worth submitting to.
routines.content:
Check every platform in the owner's tracker on the watch tier. For each, look at its current public site and terms for meaningful changes: opening to HTML5/browser games, a new developer submission program, changed rev share or exclusivity, or shutting down. Do not edit the tracker or contact anyone. If a platform looks ready to move up or should be dropped, message the owner with the platform, what changed, a source link and a recommendation, and ask for their OK before any tracker change. If nothing changed, stay silent.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 10 5 1,4,7,10 *`
